job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Dana Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Dana, and thanks for sitting down with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I share a rented room above a laundromat on Station Road in Millbrook, and I wake up to the smell of detergent. Most mornings I'm at the library by nine because the wifi at home cuts out. I send applications until lunch, then I do a few hours of unpaid chores for my flatmate Chloe to cover my share of the bills. I graduated in economics eight months ago and I've had two interviews from sixty applications.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What was your degree like, and what did you do while studying?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I did economics at Northfield University and passed with an average mark. My dissertation was on how rents and wages moved apart in our city, and I was proud of it, but I had no internship because I was stacking shelves at Fairway supermarket to pay the rent. Now I owe a huge amount in student loans and have about a week of savings, and my parents can't help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's hype, and we've heard it before, so don't waste money on it. To friends I'd say it won't fix the real problem, which is that firms won't hire people without experience. I'd probably post that online too, angrily.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my situation stays exactly as it is, and that's bad enough. Entry jobs stay scarce in Millbrook, the loan payments keep growing, and I'm still the one who 'lacks experience'. Nothing would be fixed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep sending ten applications a week to councils, housing associations and credit unions, because they at least have to follow fair hiring rules. I'd join the graduate section of the general union, which costs a few pounds a month. And I'd ask the job centre about the paid placement scheme I keep hearing about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired, mostly. It feels like standing in a queue that doesn't move, and everyone tells me to just try harder. I'm not scared of AI in this one, I'm scared of staying stuck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said nothing changes in this one. What would still be hard for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Even if AI is hype, the routine accounting admin that used to train juniors still gets handed to software a little at a time, and I notice that in the job adverts. It makes the already thin pile of entry jobs a bit thinner. The rent on my share of the room is due every month either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're already skipping some things. What goes first if money gets tighter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop buying the second-hand textbook for the professional exams I might take one day. I'd also skip the bus and walk the forty minutes to the library. Food I can't cut much more, I already eat pasta most nights. I'd never go into more debt on a card, though.

say: I'd tell people the hype is overblown and the real problem is **no entry jobs**.
I'd push for the government to fund **paid placements** for graduates.
think: Nothing fixes my situation: the **debt** keeps growing while jobs stay scarce.
Even small AI savings quietly remove some routine **entry-level** tasks from the pile.
do: Send ten applications a week to councils, credit unions and housing associations.
Join the graduate section of the general union for **a few pounds** a month.
Ask the job centre about the paid placement scheme.
feel: Tired and stuck, like a **queue** that never moves.
S0.quote: I'm not scared of AI in this one, I'm scared of staying stuck.
fieldNote: Her anger is aimed at employers and the system, not at the **technology**.
Already carries **debt** and no savings, so even a quiet scenario is stressful.
Refuses AI tools; her plan is paperwork and **group action**.

steps.text: Send ten job applications a week to councils and credit unions
Join the graduate section of the general union
Ask the job centre about the paid placement scheme

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly what unions and regulation are for. Software taking checking and booking work in firms that already pay juniors badly is not progress for us. I'd say it loudly, at the union meeting and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the door I was trying to get through closes before I reach it. Entry jobs in accounting are mostly checking invoices, matching numbers and answering simple questions, and that's the thinking work this takes first. I'd be competing against a program that doesn't need a salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still apply, but I'd widen it to jobs in the public sector, and to charities with finance admin. I'd ask Chloe to teach me her spreadsheet tricks, even though I don't use AI tools myself. I'd also try to get on a union training course for anyone who gets laid off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Angry and scared in about equal parts. I did everything I was told, a degree and loans, and the ladder gets pulled up while I'm on the second rung. I hate that it's called change when it feels like being left behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the junior accounting tasks. Which ones do you expect to go first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Reconciling bank statements, filing receipts, and preparing basic tax forms for small clients. That's what my cousin did in his first year at an accounting firm. Firms say they'll just hire fewer juniors, and nobody mentions that juniors are how seniors get made.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame if the entry jobs thin out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The firms, and the government that lets them. Companies make record profits and still won't train anyone, and ministers say 'upskill' like it's free. If the work moves to software, the firms should pay into a fund that pays for people like me to retrain or get a placement.

say: I'd say software replacing junior work needs **rules**, and firms should pay for training.
I'd tell friends the **ladder** is being pulled up on us.
think: The entry jobs I'm applying for, like checking invoices, are exactly what goes first, so I'm **competing with software**.
I blame firms and government more than the technology itself.
do: Widen applications to **public sector** and charity finance admin jobs.
Ask my flatmate Chloe to teach me her spreadsheet shortcuts.
Join a union training course for people facing redundancy.
feel: **Angry and scared**: I did everything I was told and the ladder is moving.
S1.quote: I did everything I was told, a degree and loans, and the ladder gets pulled up while I'm on the second rung.
fieldNote: Blames firms and government for ending training, not the **software**.
Her field is the first-hit desk work, and she has no **experience** to stand out.
Plans are collective and public-sector, not personal **tech skills**.

steps.text: Apply to public-sector and charity finance admin roles
Keep sending ten applications a week
Join the union training course for laid-off workers
Write to my local MP asking for a graduate placement fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say governments need to act now, with emergency income support and a freeze on student loan payments. Two years is nothing. I'd be at every meeting and march I could get to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel like I was never even given a turn. The jobs I trained for would be gone before I'd had one, and I have no savings, no family money, and no tool skills. I don't know what I'd do, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop my own job hunt in the accounting field and put my energy into the union and into any protest that asks for support payments. I'd move back into my mother's spare room if she'd have me, to stop paying rent. And I'd apply for anything with a wage, such as care work or warehouse shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicked, to be honest. I can handle a year of nothing, but not nothing with the loan growing and no plan. I'd probably cry a lot, and then get angry, and then cry again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: In two years, what happens to your loan payments and your room?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Loan payments get taken out automatically once I earn above a threshold, but if I earn nothing, interest still builds. My room is two hundred and fifty a month, and I couldn't cover it for more than a few weeks. So the move home comes fast, even though my mother's flat is tiny.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your parents that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my mum I'm sorry, that I did what everyone said and it isn't working. I wouldn't tell her how scared I am, because she's got her own worries. She'd tell me to eat something, as she always does, and that would nearly break me.

say: I'd demand **emergency income support** and a freeze on student loan payments.
I'd be at every **meeting and march** I could reach.
think: The jobs I trained for would vanish before I had my **first turn**.
I have no savings, no family money and no plan, which scares me.
do: Move back into my mother's flat within a few weeks to **stop rent**.
Apply for any wage work, such as care or warehouse shifts.
Put my energy into the **union** and protests for support payments.
feel: **Panicked**: a growing loan, no savings and no plan.
S2.quote: I can handle a year of nothing, but not nothing with the loan growing and no plan.
fieldNote: Her plan is **collective** and political, with personal fallback at her mother's flat.
The two-year warning leaves no time to act, so she moves to **survival**.
Her fear shows most when talking about her **mother**.

steps.text: Move back into my mother's spare room to stop paying rent
Join marches and union meetings calling for income support
Write to the MP demanding a loan payment freeze
Apply for care and warehouse shifts for any wage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough for governments to do something, so we should push now. I'd talk about income support, shorter work weeks and funding for retraining. I'd be loud but a bit less desperate than with two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think that's enough time to get a job and maybe keep it a few years, but not enough to build a career. The thinking jobs go in 2031 and I'd still be early in my twenties and carrying debt. I'd need to be somewhere that isn't just a desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the first job I could get, even if it's low pay, in a public office or a charity, to start earning. I'd save forty pounds a month towards a cushion and join the union properly. And I'd start learning something hands-on, maybe a trade-adjacent admin role in housing or health, because robots come later there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit calmer than with two years, but heavier too. With five years of warning, I'd have time to feel the change coming, and that's its own kind of dread.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years let you do that two years doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still refuse to use AI tools for my own work, I think. It feels like helping the thing that replaces me. But I'd admit it might be silly, since everyone around me will use it, and I'd have to at least understand it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think your view of AI would change with time to see it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The housing association where Chloe's friend works needs people for tenant support. That's a thinking job on paper, but it's about people, and those roles last longer. It pays little, but it's a start, and I could stay near my room in Millbrook.

say: I'd push for **income support** and retraining funds while there are five years to act.
I'd say we should protect people-facing jobs.
think: Five years gives me a job but not a **career**, because the thinking jobs go in 2031.
I should aim for work involving **people**, which lasts longer.
do: Take the first paid job in a public office or charity.
Save **forty pounds** a month and join the union properly.
Apply for tenant support roles at a housing association.
feel: Calmer than with two years but **heavy**, like watching a flood come up the road.
S3.quote: With five years of warning, I'd have time to feel the change coming, and that's its own kind of dread.
fieldNote: The extra time moves her from survival to a plan around **people-facing** work.
Still resistant to **AI tools** but concedes she may have to understand them.
Debt keeps her mood **high** even when she has a plan.

steps.text: Apply for tenant support jobs at a housing association
Save forty pounds a month towards a cushion
Join the union and attend its branch meetings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if people use it, and governments have no excuse not to prepare. I'd push for training that's free, and for firms to stay accountable. I'd also tell younger people not to panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be less frightened, but not calm. I'd be thirty-three by then, and I'd still have to pay off the loan and find a real career in a world where thinking work is going. Ten years makes it possible, not easy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get any paid job first, then look for a path into people-facing public work, like housing or social services. I'd study part-time for something practical, maybe a counselling or tenancy law certificate. And I'd keep up the union work, because I think that's where the real protection comes from.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful in small bursts, and angry in between. I'd feel like I have room to breathe, which I don't right now. But I'd still worry about whether anyone helps people like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With a decade, what changes about your career choices?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably finally try an AI tool, with caution, just to understand it. I've avoided it so far out of principle, but a decade is long enough that ignoring it would be silly. I'd still want rules about who it works for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want a younger graduate to hear from you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them that being angry is fine, but they should get a skill that involves people and keep a union card. I'd also say not to blame yourself for a job market that was always rigged. And I'd tell them that a pass degree is not the end.

say: I'd say ten years is a **gift**, and governments have no excuse not to prepare.
I'd push for free training and for firms to be held to account.
think: Ten years makes a career **possible, not easy**, since I'd still carry the loan.
I'm less frightened, though not calm, about whether anyone will help people like me.
do: Take any paid job first, then aim for **people-facing public work**.
Study part-time for a practical certificate in tenancy law or counselling.
Try an **AI tool** with caution, just to understand it.
feel: **Hopeful** in small bursts and angry in between, with some room to breathe.
S4.quote: I'd be thirty-three by then, and I'd still have to pay off the loan and find a real career in a world where thinking work is going.
fieldNote: With a decade she softens and considers trying **AI** for the first time.
Her ideas centre on people-facing public work and **union** protection.
Her **debt** is the constant that keeps her from calm.

steps.text: Take any paid job now to start earning
Study a tenancy law certificate part-time
Try one AI tool with caution to understand it
Keep paying union dues and attend branch meetings

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most, because I'd have no time and no money. What would help is a real income floor, a freeze on the loan payments and employers being forced to take on trainees. Also someone telling me the truth about which jobs will last.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that people like me are not lazy or stupid. Juniors with average degrees are the ones who get ignored, and we're the ones who'll feel this first. I'd want someone with power to listen.

headlineQuote: Juniors with average degrees are the ones who get ignored, and we're the ones who'll feel this first.
portrait: Dana (23) shares a rented room in **Millbrook**, owes heavy student loans and has about a week of savings.
An economics graduate with a pass and no internships, she has two interviews from sixty applications.
She is angry at firms and government, not at technology, and refuses to use **AI tools**.
Her plans are collective: **union**, politics, public-sector jobs and moving back to her mother's flat.
She is calmer only when there are years to prepare, and the debt never lets her feel safe.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture frightens her most because she'd have no time, no money and no plan.
whatWouldHelp: An **income floor**, a freeze on loan payments and employers forced to train juniors.
